text: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, but what event directly triggered the East German government's announcement opening the border?

options.B: A miscommunication at a press conference by spokesman Günter Schabowski
options.C: Helmut Kohl's televised address demanding reunification
options.D: A Supreme Court ruling by the East German judiciary

explanation: Schabowski, not fully briefed, announced the border was opening 'immediately, without delay' live on TV — sparking the rush to the Wall that night.

text: Which ancient library, often called the greatest of the ancient world, was located in Alexandria, Egypt?
explanation: Founded under the Ptolemaic dynasty around 300 BCE, it aimed to collect all the world's knowledge and held hundreds of thousands of scrolls.

text: The Marshall Plan, which rebuilt Western Europe after WWII, was named after which US Secretary of State?
explanation: General George C. Marshall proposed the European Recovery Program in a 1947 Harvard speech. It transferred ~$13B (~$140B today) to rebuild allied economies.

text: The 'Scramble for Africa' was largely formalised at which 1884–85 conference?
explanation: 14 European powers met in Berlin (Bismarck presiding) to divide Africa without African input, setting colonial borders still felt today.

text: Who led the Cuban Revolution that overthrew Batista in 1959?
explanation: Fidel Castro led the 26th of July Movement from the Sierra Maestra, entering Havana on January 8, 1959. Guevara was a key commander but not the leader.

text: The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804) was historically significant because it produced what?

options.B: The first successful slave-led revolution and first Black republic
options.C: The first constitutional monarchy in the Americas
options.D: The first democracy in the Western Hemisphere

explanation: Haiti became the only nation born from a successful slave revolt, defeating Napoleon's forces and inspiring abolitionists worldwide.

text: In what year did women gain the right to vote in the United States?
explanation: The 19th Amendment was ratified on August 18, 1920, prohibiting denial of voting rights based on sex.

text: The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) ended with which treaty, establishing the modern concept of state sovereignty?
explanation: Westphalia established that rulers had sovereignty within their own borders — the foundation of the modern nation-state system.

text: Which empire controlled the largest contiguous land area in history?
explanation: At its peak under Kublai Khan (~1279), the Mongol Empire covered ~24 million km². The British Empire was larger in total but not contiguous.

text: What was the name of the first artificial Earth satellite, launched by the Soviet Union in 1957?
explanation: Sputnik 1, launched October 4, 1957, was the size of a beach ball. Its beep over radio terrified the West and launched the Space Race.

text: DNA is composed of four bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, and what fourth base?
explanation: DNA uses thymine (T); RNA replaces thymine with uracil (U). A always pairs with T, C always pairs with G.

text: What force keeps electrons in orbit around atomic nuclei?
explanation: Electrons are negatively charged; protons are positive. The electromagnetic (Coulomb) attraction holds electrons in their orbitals.

text: Which scientist first proposed that the continents were once joined in a single landmass, a theory dismissed for decades?
explanation: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912. He was ridiculed until the 1950s–60s when seafloor spreading proved him right.

text: What is the speed of light in a vacuum, approximately?
explanation: ~299,792 km/s, rounded to 300,000 km/s. Light takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth.

text: The theory of evolution by natural selection was simultaneously and independently developed by Darwin and which other scientist?
explanation: Wallace sent Darwin a paper in 1858 describing nearly identical ideas, prompting their joint presentation to the Linnean Society.

text: What is the Higgs boson's primary role in particle physics?

options.A: Carrying the electromagnetic force between charged particles
options.B: Giving other elementary particles their mass via the Higgs field
options.C: Holding quarks together inside protons and neutrons

explanation: The Higgs field permeates space; particles that interact with it acquire mass. Confirmed at CERN's LHC in 2012.

text: What is the name for the process by which plants convert sunlight into chemical energy?
explanation: Photosynthesis converts CO₂ + H₂O + light energy → glucose + O₂, occurring primarily in chloroplasts.

text: Why does time pass more slowly in stronger gravitational fields?

options.A: Gravity slows the atoms that make up clocks
options.B: Einstein's general relativity: spacetime curves near mass, dilating time
options.C: Dense matter absorbs photons that carry time information
options.D: Time is absolute; clocks are affected by pressure, not gravity

explanation: Gravitational time dilation is real and measured — GPS satellites must correct for it or navigation errors compound at ~10km/day.

text: Which element is the most abundant in the Earth's crust by mass?
explanation: Oxygen makes up ~46% of the Earth's crust by mass, mostly bonded in silicate minerals. Silicon is second at ~28%.

text: What does the Richter scale actually measure?

options.A: The destructive power of an earthquake
options.B: The depth of an earthquake's focus
options.C: The amplitude of seismic waves (energy release)

explanation: The Richter scale measures wave amplitude on a logarithmic scale; each whole number is 10× amplitude and ~31× energy. Modern seismology uses moment magnitude (Mw).

text: Which is the longest river in the world by length?
explanation: The Nile stretches ~6,650 km; the Amazon is shorter but carries far more water by volume and has the largest drainage basin.

text: Which country has the most natural freshwater lakes in the world?
explanation: Canada holds about 60% of the world's lakes with over 2 million bodies of freshwater, more than any other nation.

text: The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20% of global oil passes, connects the Persian Gulf to which body of water?
explanation: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, which opens into the Arabian Sea — the world's most critical oil chokepoint.

text: Which continent has the highest average elevation?
explanation: Antarctica's average elevation is ~2,300 m — higher than any other continent — primarily due to the massive ice sheet piled on top of the land.

text: The Atacama Desert in South America is the driest non-polar desert on Earth. Which country does most of it fall in?
explanation: The Atacama spans ~105,000 km², mostly in northern Chile. Some areas have never recorded measurable rainfall in recorded history.

text: Which country is simultaneously in Europe, Asia, Africa and has territory in the Indian Ocean and Atlantic?
explanation: France has metropolitan territory in Europe, overseas departments in South America (French Guiana), the Caribbean, Indian Ocean (Réunion, Mayotte), and Pacific — crossing all major ocean zones.

text: What is the name of the tectonic plate boundary where two plates slide horizontally past each other?
explanation: Transform (or strike-slip) boundaries produce earthquakes but not volcanoes. The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example.

text: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds what fraction of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater?
explanation: Lake Baikal holds ~20–23% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater. It's also the world's deepest lake at 1,642 m.

text: Which ocean is the largest by surface area?
explanation: The Pacific Ocean covers ~165 million km² — larger than all Earth's landmasses combined. It contains more than half of the world's oceanic water.

text: The 'Ring of Fire' encircling the Pacific Ocean accounts for what share of the world's earthquakes?
explanation: The Ring of Fire — a 40,000 km horseshoe of active volcanoes and tectonic boundaries — produces ~90% of all earthquakes and 75% of volcanic eruptions.

text: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque jointly developed which major 20th-century art movement?
explanation: Cubism (c.1907–1922) fragmented objects into geometric forms seen from multiple angles simultaneously. Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' (1907) is often cited as the starting point.

text: In which Shakespeare play does the line 'To be, or not to be, that is the question' appear?
explanation: Hamlet's Act 3 soliloquy is perhaps the most quoted passage in English literature, contemplating the choice between suffering life or ending it.

text: The 'magic realism' literary movement is most associated with writers from which region?
explanation: Garcia Márquez, Borges, Isabel Allende, and Laura Esquivel — Latin American writers blending fantastical elements seamlessly with realistic settings.

text: Which composer was almost completely deaf when he wrote his famous Ninth Symphony?
explanation: Beethoven had been almost entirely deaf since his late 20s. He 'heard' the Ninth Symphony (1824) through vibration and musical imagination — never with his ears.

text: The Rosetta Stone, key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphics, is written in how many scripts?
explanation: The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) bears the same decree in three scripts: Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics, Demotic Egyptian, and Ancient Greek — the Greek let scholars unlock the others.

text: Which philosopher wrote 'The Republic', imagining an ideal city governed by philosopher-kings?
explanation: Plato's 'The Republic' (~380 BCE) uses Socrates as narrator but the ideas — including the Allegory of the Cave — are Plato's own.

text: Which novel begins with the line 'Call me Ishmael'?

options.A: The Old Man and the Sea

explanation: Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick' (1851) opens with one of literature's most famous first lines, narrated by the sole survivor of the Pequod.

text: The Taj Mahal was built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for whom?
explanation: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal (1632–1653) in memory of his favourite wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth. He was later buried beside her.

text: Which ancient wonder of the world was a lighthouse built on a small island near Alexandria?
explanation: The Pharos of Alexandria (~280 BCE) stood ~100–140 m tall and was among the tallest man-made structures for centuries, guiding ships into harbour with fire and mirrors.

text: The Rite of Spring premiere in 1913 caused what extraordinary reaction from the Parisian audience?

options.B: A riot — booing, fistfights, and police intervention
options.C: Complete silence for the entire performance
options.D: A walkout by the entire orchestra

explanation: Stravinsky's dissonant, primal score and Nijinsky's shocking choreography triggered one of music history's most famous riots at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées.

text: In which sport do players compete for the 'Stanley Cup'?
explanation: The Stanley Cup, donated by Lord Stanley of Preston in 1892, is the oldest professional sports trophy in North America and is awarded to the NHL champion.

text: Which country has won the most FIFA World Cup titles?
explanation: Brazil has won 5 World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002) — more than any other nation.

text: The modern Olympics were revived in 1896 in which city?
explanation: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, in April 1896, organised by Pierre de Coubertin with 14 nations competing.

text: In cricket, what is the term for a bowler taking three wickets in three consecutive deliveries?
explanation: A hat-trick in cricket predates its use in any other sport — a bowler traditionally received a hat from the club for this feat in the 19th century.

text: Michael Jordan won how many NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls?
explanation: Jordan won 6 titles in two separate three-peats: 1991–93 and 1996–98, with a 1.5-year baseball hiatus in between.

text: In tennis, what is the name for a score of 40-40 (tied at three points each in a game)?
explanation: 'Deuce' requires one player to win two consecutive points. The word derives from the French 'à deux' meaning 'to two' (points needed to win).

text: The 'Fosbury Flop' revolutionised high jump technique after Dick Fosbury won gold at which Olympics?
explanation: Fosbury's backwards-over-the-bar technique shocked the 1968 Mexico City Games; within 20 years virtually every elite high jumper had adopted it.

text: How many players are on a standard rugby union team?
explanation: Rugby union is 15 a side; rugby league is 13 a side. Both sports descended from the same game before the 1895 split.

text: Which sprinter holds the men's 100m world record, set at the 2009 World Championships in Berlin?
explanation: Usain Bolt ran 9.58 seconds in Berlin — a record that still stands and is widely considered one of the most dominant athletic performances in history.

text: What scoring system is used in a standard game of bowling?
explanation: 10 frames, 10 pins each. A perfect game (all strikes) scores 300. In the 10th frame, a strike earns two bonus rolls.

text: What is the only letter that does not appear in any US state name?
explanation: Q is the only letter absent from all 50 US state names. (Z appears in Arizona; J in New Jersey and others.)

text: How many hearts does an octopus have?
explanation: Octopuses have three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, one pumps it through the body. Their blood is blue due to copper-based haemocyanin.

text: A 'googol' is the number 1 followed by how many zeros?
explanation: A googol (10¹⁰⁰) was coined by 9-year-old Milton Sirotta in 1920. Google's name is a deliberate misspelling of googol.

text: The word 'salary' comes from the Latin word for what?
explanation: 'Salarium' — Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt or given an allowance to buy it, as salt was essential for preserving food.

text: What is the most widely spoken language in the world by total number of speakers (native + second language)?
explanation: English has ~1.5 billion total speakers (native + second-language), making it the world's most widely spoken language. Mandarin leads in native speakers only.

text: Which animal has the highest blood pressure of any mammal?
explanation: Giraffes have blood pressure nearly twice that of humans (~280/180 mmHg) to pump blood up their ~2m necks to the brain.

text: Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs was still edible after thousands of years because of honey's unique properties. What preserves it?

options.A: Its alkaline pH that kills bacteria
options.B: Its low water content, high sugar, and naturally produced hydrogen peroxide

explanation: Honey is hygroscopic (draws moisture away from bacteria), acidic (~pH 3.9), and bees add glucose oxidase which produces hydrogen peroxide — triple preservation.

text: What is the collective noun for a group of crows?
explanation: A 'murder of crows'. A group of owls is a parliament; ravens form an unkindness; starlings form a murmuration.

text: Which element was named after the Americas?
explanation: Americium (element 95) was discovered in 1944 at the University of Chicago and named after the Americas. It's used in smoke detectors.

text: The 'butterfly effect' in chaos theory was named after a paper by Edward Lorenz with what full title?

options.A: "Does the Flap of a Butterfly's Wings in Brazil Set Off a Tornado in Texas?"
options.B: "Chaos, Complexity and the Butterfly Effect in Dynamic Systems"
options.D: "The Sensitivity of the Lorenz System to Initial Conditions"

explanation: Lorenz presented this paper in 1972 at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. The title became the most famous metaphor in chaos theory.
